standard.title: Analyse and transfer movement skills
standard.description: analyse, refine and transfer movement skills in a variety of movement situations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have adapted and modified movement skills across a variety of situations and transferred familiar movement strategies to different movement contexts (Y5-6). They can identify and describe movement adjustments in response to changing conditions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse, refine and transfer movement skills across varied movement situations using feedback from multiple sources.

nodes.label: Receiving and interpreting feedback
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can receive specific movement feedback, identify what it is asking them to change, and explain the intended effect on their movement.
nodes.minimum_width: Receive feedback from one source (teacher or peer) about a specific movement in a game or activity and identify what change is being requested.
nodes.typical_width: Receive and interpret feedback from multiple sources (teacher, peer, self-review) across at least two movement contexts; distinguish between feedback that identifies a problem and feedback that prescribes a specific fix.
wider: Compare how feedback is structured and delivered differently across movement forms (e.g. teacher demonstration vs peer verbal cue vs video review) and evaluate which source was most effective for their own refinement
Explore how elite athletes in different sports structure feedback loops with coaches and reflect on how a simplified version could improve their own skill refinement process
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot interpret and act on movement feedback cannot meaningfully engage with the refinement cycle — skill analysis and transfer depend on students being able to identify what specifically needs to change and why. Without this, subsequent nodes become disconnected self-assessment.

response_modes.reason: Invest in explicitly modelling how to decode feedback — distinguish between what is described (the current movement), what is prescribed (the change), and what outcome is intended. Students need a framework for interpreting feedback, not just practice receiving it.
Encountering feedback in multiple movement forms (game-based, aquatic, dance, outdoor) builds the ability to transfer feedback interpretation across varied contexts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Feedback literacy is a transferable metacognitive skill that extends well beyond HPE — exposing students to different feedback types and sources across movement forms builds a genuinely generalisable capability.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one specific movement change implied by feedback received
Explains what improvement to the movement outcome the change is intended to produce

nodes.label: Refining movement in response to feedback
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can make a deliberate adjustment to a movement skill in response to feedback and observe whether the adjustment produced the intended change.
nodes.minimum_width: Attempt at least one movement adjustment in response to feedback and comment on whether it changed the outcome as expected.
nodes.typical_width: Make targeted adjustments across multiple refinement cycles in at least one movement context; distinguish between adjustments that improved the outcome and those that did not; explain what was different in successful refinement attempts.
wider: Refine a range of swimming strokes using feedback from teacher, peers or video resources, comparing refinement patterns across different stroke techniques
Use feedback from others to refine the composition of a group dance sequence, evaluating how individual movement refinements affected the group performance as a whole

response_modes.reason: Students need repeated refinement cycles — the skill of making deliberate adjustments and evaluating their effect improves with iteration. A single refinement attempt is not enough to build reliable self-correction habits.

success_criteria: Makes at least one deliberate movement adjustment in response to feedback
Describes whether the adjustment produced the intended change and gives a reason

nodes.label: Analysing movement skills
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can observe a movement situation and identify specific aspects of a movement skill that could be refined, with reference to what an effective version of the skill looks like.
nodes.minimum_width: Observe a movement (own or peer) and identify at least one specific aspect that affects its effectiveness, with reference to a criterion for what good execution looks like.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse movement across multiple situations and skill types; identify strengths and areas for refinement using movement criteria; link observations to specific feedback that could drive improvement.
wider: Analyse movement in peer coach scenarios — e.g. using video or live observation to diagnose movement in invasion games, swimming or gymnastics contexts, and provide targeted feedback
Compare movement analysis across game forms (net/court, invasion, striking/fielding, target) and identify how effective movement criteria differ across these forms
nodes.hinge_reason: Analysis is prerequisite to transfer — students who cannot articulate what makes a movement effective cannot strategically apply it in a new context. Transfer without analysis is pattern-matching, not the capability the descriptor requires.

response_modes.reason: Explicitly scaffold movement analysis using frameworks — e.g. task-conditions-performance criteria. Students benefit from structured observation tools before attempting unguided analysis.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one specific aspect of a movement skill that affects its effectiveness
References a criterion or benchmark for effective movement when explaining the identified area

nodes.label: Transferring movement skills to new situations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply a refined movement skill to a new or varied movement situation, adapting execution appropriately to the new context.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply a movement skill practised in one context to a different movement situation and describe one adaptation made to suit the new context.
nodes.typical_width: Transfer movement skills and strategies across a range of movement situations — including different game categories, performance contexts and outdoor/obstacle settings — explaining what was adapted and why.
wider: Use feedback from others to safely and efficiently travel around, over, up, under and through natural or built obstacles — applying movement skills learned in structured game contexts to unpredictable outdoor environments
Investigate how movement skills in one game category (e.g. invasion) transfer to a different category (e.g. net/court or target), identifying shared and divergent requirements

response_modes.reason: Transfer is the evidence of capability — students who have only practised in one context cannot demonstrate transfer. Breadth of movement contexts is not enrichment; it is the mechanism by which transfer capability is built and assessed.

This node integrates the feedback interpretation, refinement, and analysis capabilities from earlier nodes into coordinated performance across new contexts. Instruction should explicitly support students in drawing on all three in the transfer situation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Transfer is where the richest learning occurs — students encounter genuine novelty and must actively adapt rather than replicate. Width here directly generates the evidence of capability the descriptor requires.
success_criteria: Applies a movement skill from a practised context to a new movement situation
Identifies at least one adaptation made to execution to suit the new context
Uses feedback (from self or others) to evaluate whether the transfer was effective
